topic: hand papermaking: pulling sheets from the mould, couching onto felts, pressing, drying and sizing

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-4)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: digital scale wazaca gramature arkuszy; referent nieosadzony 'lift controller' z wyraznie innej dziedziny

base: I have started making paper by hand and my sheets come out very uneven.
An older mould with a finer mesh stands on the shelf above the vat.
A digital scale sits by the drying stack and weighs every sheet once dry.
The new mould gives thick corners and a thin patch across the middle.
Is that the pull through the vat, or something wrong with the mould itself?
It is almost always the pull, not the mould, at this stage of things.
Dip the mould in one smooth motion and lift it level out of the vat.
Thick corners mean you are tilting as you lift, so the pulp runs outward.
Shake the mould twice each way before the water drains right through the mesh.
Lifting level has helped and the corners are much closer to the middle now.
The sheets tear, though, when I turn the mould onto the felt to couch.
The digital scale gives eighty grams for a good sheet and sixty for a torn one.
Is the pulp too thin, or am I rolling the mould over too quickly?
Sixty grams is thin, so the sheet has too little fibre to hold together.
Add more pulp to the vat and stir it well before every second sheet.
Couch with one rolling movement from edge to edge, never straight down flat.
A damp felt releases the sheet far better than a felt that has dried out.
Stirring the vat before each sheet has made the weights far more even.
The sheets come off the mould cleanly now, with only the odd torn edge.
I tried the older mould as well and its sheets look finer and smoother.
Should I press the whole post at once, or press each sheet separately?
Press the whole post at once, because even pressure matters more than sheer force.
Build the post with felts between sheets and keep the stack square as it grows.
Bring the press down slowly, so the water leaves without dragging the fibres apart.
Ten minutes under steady pressure beats a hard squeeze that lasts one minute.
The pressed post came apart easily and the sheets held their shape well.
Drying on the line, however, several sheets curled badly along one edge.
The curled ones were all hung in the draught beside the workshop door.
Should I dry them flat between boards instead of hanging them on lines?
Drying between boards gives flatter sheets, though it takes about three times longer.
Stack the damp sheets with blotters and change the blotters twice on the first day.
Weight the stack lightly, because too much weight leaves the surface glazed and hard.
Keep the whole stack well away from that draughty door in any case.
Board drying has worked and the sheets now lie perfectly flat on the bench.
Writing ink still feathers on them, which spoils the whole point of the exercise.
I have added no size at all, since I wanted to keep things simple.
Is gelatine size worth the trouble, or is starch enough for writing paper?
Gelatine gives a harder surface and takes ink far better than starch does.
Dip each dried sheet in warm gelatine and press the post a second time.
Starch suits printing well enough, but it will not stop a wet nib feathering.
Size a few sheets both ways and write on them before committing the whole batch.
